dietEvidence.body: The teeth and jaws are consistent with carnivory, and growth-series work shows changes in mandibular force and tooth morphology through ontogeny. No gut contents are known; prey choice is inferred from anatomy and from other tyrannosaurids.

sizeNote: Length and mass are estimates from incomplete material, not measurements of a whole animal.
tagline: A tyrannosaurid from Alberta, known from many individuals across several bonebeds. The bonebeds record an accumulation, not necessarily a social group.
summary: Albertosaurus sarcophagus is an albertosaurine tyrannosaurid from the Horseshoe Canyon Formation of Alberta. The Dry Island bonebed has produced at least 26 individuals, and growth-series studies document changes in jaw force and tooth morphology. The bonebed is direct evidence of accumulation; social behaviour is an inference.

discovery.body: Named by Osborn, 1905. The record is known from Horseshoe Canyon Formation, Alberta. Numerous skulls and partial skeletons, including a growth series.

fossilEvidence.title: Preserved material
fossilEvidence.body: Numerous skulls and partial skeletons, including a growth series.

fossilEvidence.title: Stratigraphic and geographic occurrence
fossilEvidence.body: Horseshoe Canyon Formation, Alberta records the species in the Late Cretaceous. The numeric range used here is ≈77–74 Ma, an occurrence estimate rather than a direct date on every specimen.

fossilEvidence.title: Dry Island bonebed
fossilEvidence.body: The bonebed is monodominant and preserves at least 26 Albertosaurus individuals. It is the strongest population sample for the species, but the taphonomic cause of the concentration is debated.

anatomy.title: Preserved anatomy
anatomy.body: The skull is relatively gracile for a tyrannosaurid, with a narrow snout and a deep, powerful jaw.

behaviour.body: The Dry Island bonebed contains at least 26 individuals, including several growth stages. That is direct evidence of a mass accumulation, but a flood, drought or predator trap could concentrate animals that did not live as a group. Pack hunting and parental care are not demonstrated.

reconstruction.body: A licensed life reconstruction is assigned to this record and credited in Sources and credits. The species is known from numerous skulls and partial skeletons, including a growth series. The reconstruction is an artist's interpretation of appearance, not a direct observation from the fossil record; preserved integument, where present, is described in the anatomy section, and the soft-tissue outline is otherwise inferred.

confidenceNote: The skeleton and growth series are well sampled, and the Dry Island bonebed provides a population sample. The cause of the accumulation, the extent of social behaviour and the soft-tissue profile remain uncertain.
